svg.title: Bonding & properties
svg.desc: Three strong bonds: Ionic: attraction between opposite ions after electron transfer. Covalent: shared electron pairs attract both nuclei. Metallic: positive ions attract delocalised electrons. Identify the charged particles in explanations. Structure decides properties: Ionic lattices: high melting; conduct only molten or dissolved, when ions move. Small molecules: low melting/boiling; weak forces between molecules. No mobile charged particles. Giant covalent: many strong bonds → high melting. States & models: Solid: particles vibrate in fixed positions. Liquid: close particles move past each other. Gas: particles far apart, moving randomly. At a change of state, energy changes attractions/spacing, not particle identity. Model drawings simplify size, forces and movement. Metals & polymers: Metals conduct through mobile delocalised electrons; layers can slide. Different-sized alloy atoms hinder sliding. Polymers: long molecules, strong bonds along each chain, forces between chains; most are solid at room temperature. Carbon structures: Diamond: four bonds per carbon, rigid and hard, no free electrons. Graphite: three bonds; weak forces between layers let them slide. Graphene: one strong, conducting layer. Fullerenes: hollow cages; nanotubes: strong conducting cylinders. Nanoparticles: 1–100 nm: large surface area : volume ratio. Small amounts can be effective catalysts or coatings. Uses include medicine, electronics, sunscreen and antibacterial surfaces. Properties differ from bulk material; assess exposure and uncertain risks.
